dc_01: The discovery call. This happens before the demo, and it decides whether the demo even matters. You are not pitching here — you are finding the operational friction that makes one three seven obviously useful. The rule for this call: talk less than half the time.
dc_02: Beat one — open without pitching. Start with a genuine question about how their intake works today, not a feature. Something like: walk me through what happens when a potential client first reaches out. Then listen. The moment you start pitching, they stop telling you the truth.
dc_03: Beat two — learn how matters arrive. Referrals, web forms, phone calls, walk-ins? Each channel shows up in a different state of mess. You are mapping the front door, so you know where the reconstruction burden begins.
dc_04: Beat three — locate the operational friction. This is the heart of discovery. Where does a human have to gather pay stubs, rebuild a timeline, chase down missing documents? That manual assembly is exactly what one three seven removes, so find it precisely — do not settle for it's fine, we manage.
dc_05: Beat four — identify who performs it. Is it a paralegal, an intake coordinator, or the attorney themselves? Knowing who does the assembly tells you whose pain you are solving, and who your internal champion is going to be.
dc_06: Beat five — quantify the time, the delay, and the abandoned effort. How long per intake? How many days of back and forth? How many matters get half-built and then dropped? Numbers make the problem real, and later they size the value.
dc_07: Beat six — understand what the attorney needs to see first. What are the two or three things that make or break a screening decision? That is what the Decision Card should surface, so you are learning how to aim the demo before you ever open it.
dc_08: Beat seven — reflect the workflow back. Say it in their own words: so today, your coordinator spends six hours rebuilding a file before an attorney even looks at it. When a firm hears you describe their own pain accurately, you have earned the right to show the product.
dc_09: Beat eight — introduce Coverage Rate, and define it exactly, because a fuzzy metric is worse than none. Coverage Rate is the share of the firm's screening questions that the worker's submitted record can answer or meaningfully illuminate before staff reconstruction begins. It is not a judgment about whether the worker has a viable claim. Say that definition the same way every time.
dc_10: And be just as clear about what Coverage Rate is not. It is not a conversion rate, not an acceptance rate, not a win rate, and not case strength. It measures how complete the record is against the firm's own questions — nothing about the merits. If you ever hear a teammate imply it predicts case value, correct it on the spot.
dc_11: Beat nine — position one three seven narrowly. Resist the urge to make it do everything. We organize the worker's record, we link every fact to its source, and the worker chooses who sees it. That is the whole claim. A narrow, true promise beats a broad, shaky one every time.
dc_12: Beat ten — confirm whether the problem is actually meaningful to them. Ask: if that assembly work disappeared, what would it change for your team? If they shrug, they may not be a fit, and that is fine. If they lean in, you have a live opportunity.
dc_13: Beat eleven — bridge into the demo, tied to what they told you. You mentioned your paralegal rebuilds every timeline by hand — let me show you exactly that step. Now you are running the fifteen-minute demo with their own pain as the frame.
dc_14: Beat twelve — agree on a concrete next step before you hang up: a firm code, a pilot seat, or a follow-up with the attorney. And hold the discipline that runs through the whole call — you are mapping a workflow and describing a record, never diagnosing a legal claim. Locate the friction, and let the product do the rest.
